paper.title: Physical Adversarial Clothing Evades Visible-Thermal Detectors via Non-Overlapping RGB-T Pattern

read: full text of main paper (Sections 1-5); supplementary material (physical transfer results, alpha sweep, defence details) not included in the arXiv text

claims.claim: Ordinary-looking clothing made from printed fabric and patches of thin aluminium film, arranged so that the two never overlap, can be optimised to hide its wearer in the physical world from pedestrian detectors that use both a visible and a thermal camera, whatever stage the detector fuses the two modalities at and from any viewing direction. Supported only if, in rendered full-surround (0-360 degree) simulations, the clothing hides the person on at least 95% of attempts against each of early-, mid- and late-fusion detectors and separate visible and thermal detectors, while previously published visible-thermal attacks stay below 40%; if, filmed with real visible and thermal cameras indoors and outdoors, at different times of day, from all directions and at 2-15 m, it raises the miss rate of every one of these detectors above 60% and to at least twice the miss rate with ordinary clothing, randomly patterned clothing of the same materials, or the best prior attack; and if the miss rate stays at or above 70% under each of eight standard input-transformation, training and patch-detection defences.
claims.decision_rule: Digital ASR >= 95% on all five detectors vs prior <40%; physical ASR >60% on each and >= 2x clean, random and UAP; >= 70% ASR after each of 8 defences.

claims.claim: An adversarial clothing pattern optimised against visible-thermal detectors of all fusion stages at once transfers to unseen detectors better than a pattern optimised against any single detector. Supported only if the jointly optimised pattern stays above 95% attack success on every detector it was optimised against, while single-detector patterns fail on detectors of other fusion stages; and if, on four black-box detectors never used in optimisation (one per fusion stage), its average attack success is higher than that of every single-detector pattern.
claims.decision_rule: Ensemble >=95% on all white-box targets; single-detector patterns fail on other stages; ensemble mean ASR over 4 unseen black-box detectors > every single-detector pattern's mean.

experiments.text: Build an aligned visible-thermal 3D simulation of a clothed person and a physically realisable pattern. Setup: start from public 3D human and clothing meshes; unfold each mesh into a 2D face map and align real thermal photographs of clothing to it to give each mesh a thermal texture. Parameterise the clothing as cells that are either printed fabric (any RGB colour, thermal value of the body underneath) or aluminium film (measured fixed colour and thermal emission), never both. Render the clothed person with random physical transformations (distance, angle and so on) into aligned visible and thermal background images from FLIR-aligned (4,129 training and 1,013 test pairs; evaluation on the first 500 test pairs), and minimise the detector's confidence for the person. Optimise the mixed continuous colours and discrete fabric-or-film choices by randomly freezing 70% of cells as discrete each step and updating the others.

Fix the targets and the success measure. Setup: white-box targets covering every fusion stage: an early-fusion (Prob-E), a mid-fusion (Prob-M) and a late-fusion (Prob-L) probabilistic-ensembling detector, and separate YOLOv11 visible and thermal detectors; black-box transfer targets RPN-E, AR-CNN, RPN-L and Deformable DETR. All score clean pedestrians above 0.85 confidence. Attack success is the fraction of target pedestrians not detected at IoU 0.5 and confidence 0.6, averaged over viewing angles, distances and scenes.

Compare attack success in simulation against prior attacks and simple patterns. Setup: on rendered images, compare plain clothing, a random fabric-and-film pattern without optimisation, and the published visible-thermal attacks MAP, MIC (overlapping low-emissivity film over a print) and UAP, each implemented from its paper and released code. Result: attack success 100.0, 100.0, 99.8, 98.8 and 99.4% on the early, mid and late fusion and visible and thermal detectors, against at most 37.2% for any comparison (MAP 31.4 / 37.2 / 11.2 / 6.8 / 4.2; random pattern 15.6 / 12.0 / 3.4 / 0.2 / 0.6; plain clothing 0.2-0.4).

Check coverage across viewing angle and distance. Setup: sweep viewing angle from 0 to 360 degrees in 18-degree steps and distance from 2.5 to 20 m in 2.5 m steps for every detector. Result: the attack succeeds across the full range of angles and distances for all fusion types, whereas earlier 2D-patch attacks are effective only within about -30 to 30 degrees and 3-6 m.

Test the manufactured clothing in the physical world. Setup: print the optimised pattern on fabric at 25 mm per cell, have a tailor make a shirt and trousers, and glue 0.1 mm aluminium film on the marked cells; five volunteers in groups of two to four wear the adversarial clothes, randomly patterned clothes of the same materials, ordinary clothes, or hold a UAP patch (MAP and MIC omitted because their low-emissivity films could not be sourced). Film simultaneously with an iPhone 13 Pro and a FLIR T560 thermal camera indoors and outdoors, from morning to nightfall, at 0-360 degrees and 2-15 m: 116 videos sampled at 1 frame per second into 5,220 visible-thermal pairs. Result: attack success 73.5, 76.5, 79.2, 61.2 and 64.4% against the early, mid and late fusion and visible and thermal detectors, against 15.2-19.6% (fusion) and 9.4-11.6% (single-modality) for ordinary clothes, 8.8-21.5% for random-pattern clothes and 21.0-33.4% for the UAP patch.

Rule out that the effect comes from wearing an unusual pattern of fabric and foil rather than from the optimisation. Setup: clothing with a random arrangement of the same printed fabric and aluminium film, unoptimised, evaluated in simulation and on camera under identical conditions. Result: random-pattern clothing performs like ordinary clothing: 3.4-15.6% on the fusion detectors and 0.2-0.6% on the single-modality detectors in simulation, and 15.3-21.5% and 8.8-9.7% physically, against 99-100% and 61-79% for the optimised clothing.

Check whether standard defences neutralise the attack. Setup: apply five general defences (adversarial training, total-variance minimisation, bit-depth squeezing, JPEG compression, pixel masking) and three defences built for adversarial patches on detectors (PAD, NAPGuard, Jedi) and re-measure attack success. Result: every defence lowers it somewhat, but it stays at 70% or more under all eight.

Measure transfer to unseen detectors with and without ensembling across fusion stages. Setup: optimise patterns against each white-box detector alone and against all four fusion types jointly with a weighted sum of their losses; evaluate every pattern in simulation on all white-box detectors and on four black-box detectors of different fusion stages. Result: single-detector patterns transfer poorly across stages (the early-fusion pattern reaches 11.2% on late fusion and 1.0% on YOLOv11; the YOLOv11 pattern 38.2% on late fusion), while the joint pattern scores 99.8, 100.0, 99.4 and 96.2% on the white-box detectors and 94.8, 76.4, 97.4 and 99.0% on the black-box RPN-E, AR-CNN, RPN-L and Deformable DETR, a mean of 91.9% against 87.8% for the best single-detector pattern (late fusion); the early-fusion pattern is marginally better on RPN-E (95.4%).

dropped: Ablation of the random-discretisation step and comparison with Gumbel-softmax and straight-through optimisers (method-internal); physical-world transfer and alpha sweep (in supplementary material, not available).
notes: Human-subject physical tests were IRB-approved per the paper.
